quote: Problem lückenlos zusammenhängen der Körper in mehrere Dimensionen u. auf Flächen von beliebigem Geschlecht[?]
english: Problem: gap-free fitting together of bodies in several dimensions and on surfaces of arbitrary genus.
topic: A list of research problems and notes on invariant theory: gap-free assembly of bodies in several dimensions, types of linear transformations, skew invariants of binary forms of odd degree, complete systems of forms, and canonical forms.

triage.modern_statement: This is most likely an early, private version of what became Hilbert's 18th Paris problem, 'Building up of space from congruent polyhedra'. In modern terms the note asks about tilings (gap-free fillings) of n-dimensional space by congruent bodies, and of surfaces of arbitrary genus (constant-curvature geometries, i.e. spherical, Euclidean and hyperbolic). The connected questions are: (a) for each n, are there only finitely many crystallographic groups (discrete groups of isometries with compact fundamental domain), so that their fundamental domains tile space; and (b) are there polyhedra that tile space with congruent copies but are not the fundamental domain of any group of motions (anisohedral tiles)?
triage.answered_by: Not the note itself, which is a private jotting. The questions it seems to anticipate were answered within Hilbert's 18th problem (1900). Ludwig Bieberbach proved in 1910 that each n has only finitely many crystallographic groups (now called Bieberbach groups). Karl Reinhardt found a 3-dimensional tile that is not a fundamental domain of any group in 1928, and Heinrich Heesch later found a 2-dimensional one (1935 is from memory; the sources don't give the year). I found no source that discusses the 'surfaces of arbitrary genus' clause separately.

evidence.claim: Hilbert's 18th problem, 'building up of space from congruent polyhedra', asked whether there are polyhedra that are not fundamental regions of groups of motions but whose congruent copies can still fill all of space.

The first part asks whether n-dimensional Euclidean space has only finitely many essentially different groups of this kind. Bieberbach answered yes in 1910, and the groups are now called Bieberbach groups.
Reinhardt found a non-isohedral 3-dimensional tiling in 1928. Heesch later found one in 2 dimensions, a case Hilbert did not ask about.
The Heesches' work on the 18th problem concerned gap-free divisions of the unbounded plane into congruent pieces ('stones').

triage.why: The wording ('lückenlos zusammenhängen der Körper in mehrere Dimensionen', gap-free fitting together of bodies in several dimensions) closely matches the theme of Hilbert's 18th problem on filling space with congruent bodies. The mention of surfaces of arbitrary genus points to the same tiling and fundamental-domain question in spherical, Euclidean and hyperbolic geometry. The 18th problem's sub-questions on crystallographic groups and anisohedral tiles were solved by Bieberbach (1910) and Reinhardt (1928), with Heesch later finding a planar example. Confidence is medium for three reasons: the note is short, it ends with an uncertain reading ('[?]'), and no source ties this diary entry directly to the 18th problem. For 'active_today: yes' I relied on general knowledge, since none of the cited sources say tiling theory is an active field; the 2023 Heesch paper shows only that the history is still being studied.
